title: Fully dynamic near-optimal matching with polylogarithmic updates
formal: For every fixed rational \(\varepsilon \in (0,1)\), is there a randomized fully dynamic algorithm that maintains an explicit matching M with |\(M|\ge \nu (G)/(1+\varepsilon )\) in every current general graph G using polylogarithmic expected amortized update time against an oblivious adversary?
definitions: The graph is simple, undirected and unweighted, on the fixed vertex set \([n], n\ge 2; \nu (G)\) is its maximum matching cardinality. It starts empty. An update inserts one absent edge or deletes one present edge. Updates arrive online, but the entire valid sequence is fixed independently of the algorithm’s random bits and is not revealed in advance. More precisely, for every fixed \(\varepsilon\) and constant \(a\ge 1\), require constants K,d,B and a uniform randomized word-RAM algorithm \(A_{\varepsilon ,a}\) such that every sequence of \(T\le n^{a}\) updates has expected total initialization-plus-update cost at most \(K[n+T(\log _{2}(n+2))^{d}]\). Words have \(B\lceil \log _{2}(n+2)\rceil\) bits; standard word operations, memory access and retained random bits are charged. With probability at least \(1- n^{- 3}\), after every update in the sequence an explicit mate array represents a valid matching satisfying the approximation bound. Reading a vertex’s mate or the matching cardinality takes \(O(1)\) time; enumerating all matching edges costs \(O(n)\) and need not occur after every update. Changes to the mate array count toward update cost. Constants may depend on \(\varepsilon\) and a, but not on n, T or the sequence. No polynomial dependence on \(1/\varepsilon\), adaptive-adversary guarantee or worst-case per-update bound is required. The word instructions are random-access reads/writes, comparisons, conditional branches, addition, subtraction and multiplication modulo \(2^{w}\), integer quotient/remainder with nonzero divisor, bitwise Boolean operations, and shifts of a w-bit word; shifts by at least w yield zero. The constant in word length \(w=\Theta (\log  n)\) (or \(\Theta (\log  N)\) when N is the stated input size) is fixed with the algorithm. Address arithmetic has the same cost, larger integers occupy multiple words, and no instruction performs arbitrary-precision arithmetic in one step. When randomization is allowed, a fresh independent uniform w-bit word costs one operation. In this statement, “explicitly given/encoded/listed” means the entire finite list, table or syntax tree described above is part of the input or output, with its full encoding counted; it does not mean a circuit, oracle or program generating a larger object.
answer_criterion: Prove the proposition in the problem statement or prove its logical negation, using exactly the definitions, hypotheses and quantifier order stated here. The proof must cover the complete target.
why: The principal update-time frontier for maintaining actual near-optimal matchings under arbitrary edge insertions and deletions, beyond maximality and matching-size estimation.

importance.reason: A central dynamic graph problem connecting approximation, explicit solution maintenance and extremal induced-matching structure.

progress.text: Polylogarithmic-update algorithms beat factor two for matching-size estimation; SODA 2024 extends the \(2- \sqrt{2}- \eta\) fraction to general graphs.
Liu obtains \(n/2^{\Omega (\sqrt{\log  n})}\) update time for near-optimal bipartite matching, with polynomial accuracy dependence and connections to online matrix-vector problems.
Behnezhad–Ghafari introduce the ordered-RS route; Assadi–Khanna–Kiss improve its update bound to roughly \(n^{o(1)}\) times the relevant ORS count.
Pratt connects polynomial-density ordered and ordinary RS graphs; the result appears at SOSA 2026.
Chuzhoy–Khanna–Song post a deterministic \(n^{1/2+o(1)}\)-update maximal-matching algorithm, presented at STOC 2026. This is a weaker approximation target.

status_note: Reviewed through 11 September 2026. No polylogarithmic-update algorithm meeting the fixed-accuracy, explicit-matching target was found. Matching-size estimators, ordered-RS-dependent bounds and the 2026 maximal-matching improvement do not resolve it.

context_blocks.text: A maximum matching allocates the largest possible number of disjoint pairs. When an edge changes, recomputing it from scratch ignores the substantial information retained from the preceding graph. The dynamic problem asks how much of that information can be reused while keeping a solution within an arbitrarily small fixed relative loss of optimum. Both insertions and deletions are allowed, so previously useful structure can disappear.

The graph’s optimum changes by at most one after a single edge update, but a particular solution may require coordinated replacements. On a long alternating path, gaining one additional matched edge can involve changing many pairs. Approximation creates room to postpone or distribute some repairs. The difficulty is to do so without accumulating a large loss or spending too much time discovering the repairs that are needed.

An explicit solution is part of the target. A number close to \(\nu (G)\) need not identify even one edge that can safely be used with the others. A mate array makes this distinction observable: a query at a vertex must return its current partner or report that it is unmatched. Requiring the whole array to be printed after every update would impose an artificial linear output cost, so the formulation instead charges only actual changes and queries.

Maximality is also weaker than near-optimality. In a four-vertex path, selecting only the middle edge gives a maximal matching of size one, while the two outside edges give a maximum matching of size two. Randomized maximal-matching algorithms already achieve very small update times against oblivious sequences. Chuzhoy–Khanna–Song’s STOC 2026 result improves deterministic maximal matching to \(n^{1/2+o(1)}\) amortized time; its guarantee still concerns maximality.

A separate sequence of breakthroughs beats the factor-two barrier for estimating matching size in polylogarithmic update time. Azarmehr–Behnezhad–Roghani’s SODA 2024 result obtains an estimate corresponding to a \(2- \sqrt{2}- \eta\) fraction of optimum in general graphs, for fixed \(\eta >0\). The paper explicitly studies size estimation. Its title alone can therefore suggest a stronger maintenance result than the theorem actually supplies.

For maintaining actual near-optimal matchings, Assadi–Khanna–Kiss’s SODA 2025 work develops a connection to ordered Ruzsa–Szemerédi graphs. Such a graph has its edges partitioned into matchings, with each matching induced in the union of itself and later matchings. Dense examples quantify how often certain expensive matching searches can recur. Their update bound is expressed through this extremal quantity and works even against adaptive adversaries.

The dependence is roughly \(n^{o(1)}\) times the ordered-RS count for matchings of linear size, with accuracy-dependent parameters. A strong enough combinatorial upper bound would yield subpolynomial update time. This does not currently establish polylogarithmic time: \(n^{o(1)}\) can grow faster than every fixed power of log n, and the required extremal bounds are themselves unresolved. This connection is not an unconditional lower bound.

Pratt’s SOSA 2026 note relates the ordered and ordinary RS notions at the level of polynomial exponents. Dense ordered examples would imply nearly comparably dense ordinary examples. It resolves a structural question about the reduction’s graph families, but does not determine the density needed for a polylogarithmic dynamic algorithm.

Liu’s 2024 work gives a different advance for bipartite graphs: amortized update time \(n/2^{\Omega (\sqrt{\log  n})}\) times a polynomial in \(1/\varepsilon\). It also relates stronger update bounds to online matrix-vector problems. The dependence on accuracy is essential in those statements. In particular, the ordinary-OMv equivalence stated for approximate vertex cover should not be silently transferred to matching, and a barrier using inverse-polynomial accuracy does not settle this card’s fixed-\(\varepsilon\) question.

The adversary convention leaves useful flexibility. An oblivious sequence may be carefully chosen to be difficult, but it cannot react to random decisions or the current matching. The algorithm nevertheless receives updates one at a time; knowing that the sequence was fixed does not give access to future deletions. Similarly, amortization permits occasional expensive repairs as long as their expected total cost satisfies the bound.

The inherited Max Planck report explicitly identifies near-optimal fully dynamic matching with polylogarithmic updates as a long-term target. Its page 123 also distinguishes maintaining matching edges from estimating their number, and describes faster progress in the insertion-only setting. Allowing deletion of a vertex, which removes all its incident edges together, does not automatically supply an algorithm for arbitrary individual edge deletions.

The fundamental issue is whether a changing combinatorial optimum can be tracked almost as cheaply as the graph itself is updated. A positive result would close a major gap between coarse approximation and near-optimal explicit solutions. It would also clarify how much global matching structure must be recomputed when each input change is local.

sentences: A matching selects graph edges without shared endpoints.
The reviewed question asks to maintain an explicit matching within a factor of one plus \(\varepsilon\) of maximum using polylogarithmic expected amortized update time.
Although the optimum changes little after one update, repairing a particular matching may involve a long alternating path.
A solution would combine nearly optimal allocation quality with efficient response to both insertions and deletions.
The saved record requires actual partner information and distinguishes this task from estimating matching size or maintaining the weaker guarantee of maximality.
